newsitem.title: USA: TALKING POINT/Xerox bounce seen taking longer. [CORRECTED 07:01 GMT 19/10]
newsitem.headline: TALKING POINT/Xerox bounce seen taking longer. [CORRECTED 07:01 GMT 19/10]

text.p: After Xerox Corp's stunning third quarter earnings disappointment on Friday and a string of earlier letdowns, it will be at least three quarters before the copier company redeems itself on Wall Street. Investors who

watched Xerox stock fall as low as 46-1/4 from 57 in unusually vigorous trading could draw some solace knowing that Xerox shares have rebounded from prior, disappointment-driven sell-offs, analysts said.

"It was not a matter of lack of demand for equipment, it was a matter a matter of what price they sold at. So the problem is a field pricing and that takes takes three or four quarters to play through," Henderson said.
He said his buy recommendation remains unchanged, though he "expects the stock to tread water for the next six to nine months".

Ty Govatos, analyst with Donaldson Lufkin & Jenrette, said in a research note that in each of the last three years, Xerox has thrown investors with at least one negative results surprise, and each time the stock was pummeled, but then recovered.
"Those declines have proven to be good buy points," he wrote, noting Xerox at 49 to 50 per share "represent a good buy point for short-term trading accounts."
He noted that there is "always a risk the the decline in B&W copiers represents a secular slowing, but that is not likely and revenues should experience some rebound in the fourth quarter."

"The black-and-white copier decline occurred not only in the U.S. but also in Europe and Brazil. Brazil, which always has been unpredictable, may stay at current levels for some quarters to come so we are lowering our 1996 and 1997 estimates by $0.15 per share," Govatos wrote.
His new new estimates are $3.35 per share in 1996 and $3.85 per share in 1997, while the market performer rating was unchanged.
Salomon Bros' Jonathan Rosenzweig (corrects analyst's name) and Deutsche Morgan Grenfell's Rudolf Hokanson said the main element of their Xerox investment thesis is the digital business.
"I think the stock is attractive at the these prices, and it is the same story in terms of being attractive becasue of the growth in the digital markets," Hokanson said.
The bright point in the generally dismal announcement was news of a 23 percent rise in Xerox's digital enterprise printing revenues, which includes color copiers.
The rise exceeded Rosenzweig's estimate by three percent.
